fixes.explanation: A house, yes. At Succoth, Jacob builds a house for himself and shelters for his livestock (Genesis 33:17). The animals get shelters and Jacob gets a roof of his own. After my years in the back of a junk drawer, a house sounds like a palace to me, baker.

Leah is in the lineup, friend, just not at the rear. The text puts the maidservants and their children in front, Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear (Genesis 33:2). Leah is Jacob's wife, and she's in the middle spot. The very back belongs to Rachel and Joseph.

Zilpah is a name from earlier in Jacob's story, but this passage doesn't name the maidservants. It only says the maidservants and their children go in front, with Leah and her children next, and Rachel and Joseph at the rear (Genesis 33:2). With so many people in this lineup, it's easy to lose track, baker. Rachel is the one at the back.

Jacob did work hard for Laban, his father-in-law (Genesis 31:38-41), but that's not what he says here. He says, "These are the children God has graciously given your servant." (Genesis 33:5). Graciously means a gift, not a paycheck. Jacob keeps the credit with God.

That's it, baker. Jacob says, "To find favor in your sight, my lord…" (Genesis 33:8). Think about that. Esau came with four hundred men, and Jacob calls him "my lord" and asks for his favor. I've handed over a warm cookie to win somebody over, but this is a whole company of gifts. It's a humble way to walk up to his brother.

Shechem is a city Jacob reaches after Succoth, where he camps just outside it (Genesis 33:17-18). It's not the place named for the livestock shelters, though. That name is Succoth (Genesis 33:17). Right area, next stop on the map, friend.

No gate shows up in this passage. On the plot he bought, the text says Jacob set up an altar and called it El-Elohe-Israel (Genesis 33:20). A gate isn't mentioned in the verse, so the altar is our answer, friend.
